query: Prior calculations on concentrated alloys examined variations in atomic mass and force constants, temperature-dependent lattice heat transport, or DFT-derived elastic properties coupled to analytical conductivity estimates; some estimates require a Debye temperature. The cited simulations generally represented perfect, defect-free bulk crystals. Experiments below 200 K indicate that lattice and electronic contributions in HfNbTaTiZr can be comparable, while measurements from 300 to 1200 K on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen report total conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m). Available analytical approaches do not capture all relevant atomic-scale complexity in refractory high-entropy alloys, and separate transport studies do not establish a predictive solution for this alloy. Given these constraints, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified new predictive approach make for HfNbTaTiZr without conflating lattice and electronic heat transport? Explain why it should outperform earlier approaches, quantify the expected improvement, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting observations from the cited work, and specify decisive comparisons with low- and high-temperature measurements that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A new multiscale predictive model that decouples the phonon (lattice) and electronic contributions in HfNbTaTiZr by explicitly incorporating the local force‐constant disorder and anharmonicity (via quantum-informed phonon lifetime calculations) will predict the lattice thermal conductivity with a substantially lower error than earlier Debye or homogenized MD models. Specifically, for nearly defect-free, low‐oxygen samples, this approach will yield lattice conductivity predictions that are approximately 30% more accurate over the 300–1200 K range, and separately predict a lattice conductivity component that remains nearly constant above room temperature, while leaving the electronic part to be independently estimated.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase, defect-free HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy with minimal oxygen contamination (<0.1 wt.%).
generation.intervention: Application of a new predictive framework that couples quantum-derived phonon lifetime and anharmonicity calculations (capturing the effect of force-constant fluctuations from chemical disorder) with machine-learning predictions for elastic constants, treating lattice and electronic heat transport separately.
generation.conditions: Predictions are to be made for well-prepared bulk samples in the temperature range of 300 K to 1200 K, where the electronic conductivity already dominates total measured values; the approach is not conflating contributions and is intended for oxygen-free or controlled oxygen content specimens.
generation.structural_mediator: The local atomic-scale disorder that causes significant force-constant fluctuations in the BCC matrix, leading to enhanced phonon scattering and altered phonon lifetimes.
generation.mechanism: By explicitly accounting for chemical disorder at the microscopic level (i.e. variations in mass and force constants) and their impact on anharmonic phonon interactions, the model decouples the intrinsic lattice vibrational contribution from the electronic contribution. This is achieved through improved phonon lifetime calculations (beyond simple Debye estimates) and separate ML-calibrated elastic property predictions which inform the lattice dynamics.
generation.predicted_outcome: The model should predict a lattice thermal conductivity that exhibits a weak temperature dependence above room temperature (consistent with experimental observations for oxygen-controlled specimens) and quantitatively differs by around 2–3 W/(K·m) (i.e. ~30% improved accuracy) from earlier homogenized approaches. Decisive tests include comparing predicted lattice conductivity values against low-temperature (≈200 K) separable measurements and high-temperature (300–1200 K) total conductivity measurements (with electronic part subtracted via independent estimation).
generation.baseline: Existing predictive methods based on Debye approximations or small-scale MD simulations generally neglect detailed force-constant disorder and anharmonic effects, leading to approximately 20–30% errors in estimating the lattice contribution when compared to experiments.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to pristine, bulk HfNbTaTiZr alloys; its predictive improvements may not hold for samples with significant defect structures, high oxygen content, or under extreme processing conditions that introduce additional scattering centers beyond chemical disorder.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative improvement (≈30% error reduction) and the weak temperature dependence prediction rely on combining findings on phonon broadening due to force-constant fluctuations (e.g., PMC9726824’s discussion on HEA phonon behavior) with the separate treatment of disordered elastic properties in Hf-based HEAs (e.g., PMC10254787’s MD studies). The integration of quantum-derived anharmonicity with ML elastic predictions is new, and its performance in decoupling electronic and lattice contributions remains to be validated.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate a series of high-purity, oxygen-controlled HfNbTaTiZr samples and measure their total thermal conductivity over the temperature range 200–1200 K. Independently determine the electronic contribution (e.g., via Lorenz number/Wiedemann–Franz analysis or terahertz spectroscopy). Compare the separated lattice conductivity with the predicted temperature dependence and magnitude from the new approach.
measurements: Electrical conductivity (σ) to estimate κelectronic via Wiedemann–Franz law
Microstructural and compositional analysis to ensure defect-minimal, low-oxygen state
Phonon lifetime or dispersion measurements (e.g. via inelastic neutron/X-ray scattering)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the measured lattice thermal conductivity either does not exhibit the predicted weak temperature dependence or deviates by more than ±30% from the model predictions (after independently subtracting the electronic part), then the hypothesis that the decoupled predictive approach yields a substantial accuracy improvement would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In order to obtain a HEA composition that reduces the density of the alloy while retaining the strength as much as possible, this paper attempts to explore the effect of reducing the proportion of high-density elements, Hf and Ta, on the mechanical properties of HfNbTaTiZr HEAs. By individually adjusting the ratio of one element to conduct MD simulations, the effects of Hf and Ta elements on the mechanical properties of high-entropy alloys were investigated separately. The room temperature tensile stress–strain curves obtained by MD simulation are shown in Figure 4a,b. The crucial point of our approach is to enhance the simulation efficiency by employing the most suitable method for different sets of properties. Specifically, CPA’s quantum mechanical treatment of solid solutions and its analytical nature eliminates finite-size cell effects and sampling errors related to random atomic configurations, making it excel in calculations of the concentration dependence of properties that are relatively insensitive to local relaxations, such as elastic constants and misfit volumes. In comparison to supercell calculations with MLIPs, CPA is especially superior in accuracy when dealing with abrupt changes of the Fermi-surface topology, which is often encountered in bcc alloys and can have a significant impact on the concentration dependence of properties. On the other hand, ab initio based MTP methodology surpasses CPA in dealing with defects and special geometries, such as surfaces, due to its capability to incorporate local atomic relaxations.

Thermal conductivity (κ) is usually divided into two components, the electronic thermal conductivity (κe) and the lattice thermal conductivity (κg). Direct experimental separation of these two components is not feasible. Thus, to the first order approximation, κe is usually estimated based on the Wiedemann-Franz relationship where L is the Lorentz constant of 2.45 × 10−8 W Ω K−2 .

Recently, a new family of crystalline metallic materials has been discovered and has come to the forefront of materials research for their exceptional mechanical properties: High-Entropy Alloys (HEAs). Obtained with casting techniques from the melt, HEAs are single-phase, equiatomic alloys with four or more elements that are evenly dispersed in an average ordered, close-packed, and simple crystalline structure, forming a random solid solution,. The strong chemical disorder within the unit cell introduces disorder at a larger lengthscale, as the periodically repeated unit cell is in fact always different due to the random atomic arrangement within it. As such, the translational invariance is disrupted, drawing these materials closer to glasses. Indeed, HEAs share with these latter the presence of a distribution in atomic sizes, masses and force-constants, usually absent or present only in a limited extent in crystalline materials. Moreover, HEAs also exhibit thermal transport properties quite similar to glasses: thermal conductivities that are much lower than in simple metals, going from some tens of W/mK down to less than 2 W/mK, and a low and almost temperature independent lattice
